what_it_does: Running AI models requires billions of multiplications, and multiplier circuits eat a lot of chip area and power. One clever alternative is to precompute answers and store them in a lookup table (LUT): instead of multiplying two numbers, you look up the pre-stored result — much like a times-table on paper. The MADDNESS algorithm formalizes this idea for neural-network weight multiplications. This paper builds a fully digital chip around that concept, meaning it avoids the analog-to-digital converters that earlier MADDNESS implementations needed, which were bulky and sensitive to manufacturing variation. It also adds a self-synchronous pipeline accumulator: a design where the circuit signals its own readiness rather than relying on a shared clock signal, which shrinks the clock-distribution wiring and makes the chip more robust to temperature and voltage swings. Simulated in a 22-nanometer chip process, the design reportedly achieves 2.5 times better energy efficiency and 5 times better area efficiency than prior approaches.
